forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Durham highways overspent by £1.192m in 2025/26, driven by £3.334m on road defect repairs
news_drafts.lead:
Durham County Council's highways service overspent its day-to-day budget by £1.192m in 2025/26, according to a report to the Environment and Sustainable Communities Overview and Scrutiny Committee, which met on 2 October. Day-to-day spending (revenue spending) covers staff, services and contracts, as opposed to spending on things that last.

The report says the overspend was mainly due to £3.334m spent over budget on highways maintenance, specifically repairing defects in the road network. It describes this as "a recurring issue for several years". Where the work qualified, the council paid for £1.8m of the repairs as capital spending, which is money spent on things that last, such as roads. That left £1.534m of the defect repair overspend falling on the day-to-day budget.

For the structural gap in the highways budget, the council plans a new Land Rental Scheme, which the report says will start in 2026/27.

news_drafts.headline: County Durham Council assessed as a "going concern" on 31 July, with no significant risks identified
news_drafts.lead:
County Durham Council's Corporate Director of Resources concluded on 31 July 2026 that the council can be treated as a "going concern", meaning an organisation expected to keep operating, which is the basis on which its formal annual accounts (the statement of accounts) are prepared. The assessment found the council has "a history of stable finance and ready access to financial resources in the future".

It also found no significant financial, operating or other risks that would jeopardise the council's continuing operation, and that the accounts could be prepared on that basis. The papers record the conclusion only. They put no figures on it.

The assessment is set out in the annual report of the council's Audit Committee, covering September 2025 to August 2026, which was before the committee at its meeting on 30 September 2026.
news_drafts.paper_title: 06 Annual Report of the Audit Committee for the period September 25 to August 26

news_drafts.headline: County Durham's schools high needs overspend was £16.7m in 2025-26 against £14.25m budgeted
news_drafts.lead:
County Durham's spending on support for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) overspent by £16.742m in 2025-26, the Children and Young People's Overview and Scrutiny Committee was told on 25 September. The council had budgeted for a deficit of £14.250m on the high needs part of the dedicated schools grant (the government money that funds schools, with high needs covering children with SEND). The outturn, the actual figures once the year had ended, was £2.492m worse. The overall schools-funding deficit stood at £36.080m at the year end, up from £20.229m.

The papers attribute part of the overspend to alternative provision, which exceeded budget by £1.754m, and to post-16 independent and non-maintained special schools, which overspent by £0.830m because demand was higher than anticipated. For 2026-27, the council set the high needs budget with a deficit of £30.278m. The first-quarter forecast is £31.105m, or £0.827m higher, because of more special school places and higher costs for pupils with complex needs. On that forecast the cumulative deficit reaches £67.185m by 31 March 2027.

The council submitted its Local SEND Reform Plan to the Department for Education in June 2026. Once the plan is assessed and approved, funding of up to 90% of the £36.080m deficit, or £32.472m, would be paid to the council, leaving about £3.6m. The statutory override, a temporary government rule that keeps such deficits off the main balance sheet, expires on 31 March 2028, when the paper says central government assumes responsibility for SEND funding.

findings.committee: Charter Trustees for the City of Durham
findings.headline: General reserve balance projected to fall from £54,244 to £46,250 as reserves are drawn down by £7,994 instead of a planned £156 contribution.
findings.detail: The Charter Trustees' general reserve stood at £54,244 at 1 April 2026. Due to the projected overspend of £8,150, the budget will require a drawdown from reserves of £7,994 rather than the originally planned contribution of £156. This results in the reserve balance decreasing to £46,250 at 31 March 2027.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdowns indicate financial pressure and reduced financial resilience; finance officers track reserve movements to assess whether an authority can manage unexpected pressures.
findings.figures: General reserve balance: £54,244 (1 April 2026) to £46,250 (31 March 2027); drawdown of £7,994 vs planned contribution of £156; net movement of £8,150
findings.quote: The general reserve balance at 1 April 2026 was £54,244. With a projected overspend of £8,150, the amount required to be drawn from reserves would be £7,994, rather than the original budget figure of £156 contributed to reserve. Consequently, the reserve balance would decrease to £46,250 as at 31 March 2027.

findings.committee: Charter Trustees for the City of Durham
findings.headline: Charter Trustees project an £8,150 overspend (10.8%) for 2026/27, primarily driven by a £9,000 (35.4%) overspend on civic car transport costs.
findings.detail: The projected net expenditure is £83,480 against a budget of £75,329. The main variance is the civic car at £20,000 against a budget of £11,000. This overspend is attributed to the timing of invoicing, as five quarterly invoices will be paid in 2026/27 following a delayed bill from the prior year.
findings.matters: Budget variances of this magnitude (35.4%) on controllable costs highlight the importance of invoice management and forecasting accuracy.
findings.figures: £8,150 overspend on £75,329 budget (10.8% variance); civic car £20,000 outturn vs £11,000 budget; £9,000 overspend (35.4% variance)
findings.quote: The transport outturn figure at 31 March 2027 is projected to be £25,400; an overspend of £9,000 (35.4%) in comparison to the annual budget.

findings.paper_title: Council 21.10.26 - Annual Report of the Audit Committee for the period September 25 to August 26
findings.headline: Audit Committee operating one member below required strength after May 2026 AGM
findings.detail: The Audit Committee should comprise nine elected members under its Terms of Reference. Following the May 2026 AGM, one newly appointed member was unable to take up their position, leaving the Committee with eight members. Officers are working to fill the vacancy.
findings.matters: An understrength governance committee reduces scrutiny and independent oversight of controls and risk; lenders assess governance capacity and independence as indicators of board effectiveness.
findings.figures: Current membership 8 of 9 required; vacancy identified May 2026
findings.quote: only eight elected members have been appointed to date following the Annual General Meeting of the County Council in May 2026, as one of the newly appointed members was unable to take up their position

findings.paper_title: Council 21.10.26 - Annual Report of the Audit Committee for the period September 25 to August 26
findings.headline: Council confirmed as going concern with stable finances and ready access to financial resources, no material risks identified
findings.detail: In July 2026, the Council assessed itself as a going concern with a history of stable finance and ready access to future resources. The assessment concluded no significant financial, operating or other risks would jeopardise continuing operation.
findings.matters: Going concern assessment is fundamental to financial reporting credibility and lender confidence. A clean assessment confirms the Council is not at risk of inability to meet obligations or service delivery.
findings.figures: Assessment made 31 July 2026 for accounts year ending 31 March 2026
findings.quote: The assessment concluded that the Council has a history of stable finance and ready access to financial resources in the future. It was also felt there are no significant financial, operating or other risks that would jeopardise the Council's continuing operation

findings.paper_title: Council 21.10.26 - Annual Report of the Audit Committee for the period September 25 to August 26
findings.headline: Council facing increasing cost pressures in Children in Care placements; presented mitigation arrangements
findings.detail: In February 2026, the Audit Committee received a presentation on factors driving rising costs in Children in Care, including use of unregulated and crisis placements. The Council outlined controls and actions being taken to manage and mitigate these pressures.
findings.matters: Children's services represents a significant uncontrollable cost area for councils; rising placement costs are a budget risk. Finance directors and lenders need to understand whether pressures are contained within budgets or represent emerging deficits.
findings.figures: Presentation covering unregulated and crisis placement arrangements; specific costs not disclosed in Audit Committee report
findings.quote: provided an overview of the factors driving the increasing cost pressures associated with Children in Care and the action the Council was taking to manage and mitigate those cost pressures
